Wikipedia's internal infrastructure is just as fascinating as it's massively-interconnected-connectome-like front-facing system... however i'm curious about one particular infrastructural problem, becuase it reveals whether systems are scaleable, by individuals or by teams, when and why to use each model.

In Knowledge work (I hypothesize, based on extensive experience with complex knowledge bases) there are 2 primary structures for organizing (which is realy a subset of categorization... but that is a discussion for a separate channel...) information:

- Hierarchical
    
- Topological
    

Isn't a system harder to maintain, standardize and author if it is topological,as compared to hierarchical? For example, organizing all articles under "Thermodynamics"

However, the Topological network model posesses one structural quality which the Hierarchy classicaly cannot achieve; "Multi-category" This appears to be closer to how we as Human beings organize and categorize parts and information about the world and Phenomena (unsure if connectomes are relevant here...)

Here is the hybrid model: Hierarchy as a base of distribution of power and inheritance + associative links + database properties per file.

## Formula
We may even sketch a relational formula: As the system increases in abstract units of information, the underlying base model (hierarchical, topological, ...) largely determines the distribution of power: categorization, rename, delete, merge, these are essentially 'operations' of information and knowledge... and it's essential to higher-order intelligence, e.g., neuroplasticity.
